reason: At src/git-auth.ts:8, gitAuthArgs decides whether to attach the service token with `remoteUrl.includes("github.com")`. That is a substring check on the whole URL. It does not parse the URL or compare the hostname. When it matches, the function returns `-c http.extraHeader=Authorization: Bearer ${token}`. In src/worktree.ts:15, cloneRepo passes repo.remoteUrl to gitAuthArgs together with SERVICE_TOKEN, which config.ts:4 reads from HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, and then runs `git clone` against that same URL. The only caller is registerRepo in src/routes.ts:19-22. It takes remoteUrl from req.body and checks only that the value is non-empty before calling cloneRepo. There is no allowlist, no URL parsing and no host validation anywhere on this path. Any URL that contains "github.com" anywhere gets the token, and git sends that header to whatever host the URL names. Examples are `https://github.com.evil.example/x.git` and `https://evil.example/github.com/x.git`. F08, F09 and F18 all describe this same defect.

evidence.code: export const SERVICE_TOKEN = process.env.HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN ?? "";

failure_scenario: An authenticated user calls registerRepo with body {id: "x", remoteUrl: "https://github.com.attacker.example/x.git"}. routes.ts passes the URL to cloneRepo without validating it. gitAuthArgs matches the substring "github.com" and returns the Authorization header option. git then clones from github.com.attacker.example, and each HTTPS request carries `Authorization: Bearer <HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN>`. The attacker's server logs the header and ends up with the service's GitHub token.
severity_reason: Any user who can register a repository can steal the service-wide GitHub credential with one request. With that token they get whatever GitHub access the service has, across every repository it can reach. It is an easily exploited credential leak.

reason: The issue is real for the current-user fetch, but not for the user-list fetch. In src/api.ts, fetchCurrentUser (line 13) passes the response to json(), and json() throws `HTTP ${status}` for any non-2xx response (line 7). A network error from fetch also propagates. loadDashboard awaits fetchCurrentUser at line 27 with no try/catch. The only caller, mountDashboard in src/dashboard.ts:5, starts it with `void loadDashboard(...)` and attaches no .catch. So when /api/me fails, the promise rejection goes unhandled, render is never called, and the root element stays at "Loading..." forever. Nothing in the repo handles unhandledrejection. F02's claim about fetchUserList is wrong: lines 17-23 wrap the request in try/catch and return [] when !res.ok or on any exception, so it never throws. For the same reason, F03's "either one" is only half right. "Crash" overstates the effect: the page does not blow up, it just hangs on the loading text with no error shown.
failure_scenario: A user's session expires and GET /api/me returns 401. json() in src/api.ts:7 throws "HTTP 401", and the rejection passes through loadDashboard at line 27 to `void loadDashboard(...)` in src/dashboard.ts:5, where nothing catches it. The rejection goes unhandled, render never runs, and the dashboard stays at "Loading..." with no error message and no redirect to login.
severity_reason: This only happens when /api/me fails (expired session, server error or network failure), which is a failure path, not the normal flow. The result is a dashboard stuck on "Loading..." plus an unhandled rejection. No data is lost or corrupted and there is no security impact. The user-list half of the claim is false because fetchUserList already handles its errors.

reason: Nothing in the repository checks the repository id. registerRepo (src/routes.ts:18-23) only checks that `id` and `remoteUrl` are non-empty. It saves the id and passes it to cloneRepo. cloneRepo calls cachePath (src/worktree.ts:9-11), which returns `path.resolve(REPOS_DIR, id)`. An id such as `../../../tmp/x` or `/tmp/x` therefore sends the git clone to a directory outside /var/harbor/repos. The template route (src/routes.ts:35-40) builds `base` from the raw `req.params.id`. Its `startsWith(base)` check only compares the file path against that base, which the attacker also controls. If the id resolves to a higher directory, the check still passes and the route reads any file under that directory. cacheListing (line 60) resolves the raw id with the same cachePath helper. Store.insertRepo stores the id as given, and no other file contains validation or router middleware. CLAUDE.md is not in the working tree, so F14's appeal to "invariant 1" has no support. The missing validation it describes is still real.

evidence.code: export const REPOS_DIR = "/var/harbor/repos";

failure_scenario: A user calls the template route with id `../../..` (URL-encoded if the router needs it) and name `../etc/passwd`. `base` becomes `/`, `file` resolves to `/etc/passwd`, `startsWith("/")` passes, and the route returns the file's contents. With id `..` and name `../audit.log`, the same route returns /var/harbor/audit.log, which bypasses the admin IP check in auditLog. Separately, POST registerRepo with body id `/tmp/evil` clones the attacker's repository to /tmp/evil instead of a folder under /var/harbor/repos.
severity_reason: This is a security flaw that can be exploited: a caller can read files anywhere on the server and write clones outside /var/harbor/repos. I rated it High rather than Critical because the router and authentication layer are not in the repository. How URL params are decoded and who can reach these routes cannot be confirmed from the code. The registerRepo write outside the repositories directory uses the request body, so it does not depend on the router.

reason: In src/store.ts, Store.deleteRepo sends admins down an unrestricted DELETE (line 26). For everyone else it runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')` (line 29). The `OR owner = 'system'` clause means a non-admin's delete matches both their own rows and every row owned by 'system'. The route handler in src/routes.ts, deleteRepo (lines 26-33), does no check of its own. It passes req.params.id and req.user straight to store.deleteRepo, and the only guard left is the SQL filter. Nothing else in the repository limits this: there is no role check, no middleware in routes.ts, no test, and no comment saying non-admins should be able to delete system repos. The admin/non-admin split shows the non-admin branch is meant to be owner-scoped, and the extra clause breaks that. Both findings describe the same defect: F13 covers the route that reaches it and F16 covers the filter.
failure_scenario: A shared repository row exists with owner 'system'. An authenticated user with oid 'u123' and isAdmin=false calls the deleteRepo route with that repo's id. src/routes.ts:28 calls store.deleteRepo(id, {oid:'u123', isAdmin:false}). The SQL at src/store.ts:29 matches because owner = 'system', so the row is deleted, changes is 1, and the route returns 204. The shared repository is now gone for every user.
severity_reason: This is a broken authorization check that lets any authenticated user permanently delete shared system repositories, which is data loss. I rated it High rather than Critical because nothing in this repository creates rows owned by 'system': registerRepo always sets owner to req.user.oid. So the impact depends on system rows being seeded somewhere outside this code.

reason: In src/ci.ts:4, `getBuild` calls `fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`)` with no options: no `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, and nothing wraps it in a timeout. The only caller is the `build` route handler in src/routes.ts:52, which awaits `getBuild` directly and has no timeout, race, or abort of its own. I searched src for a global dispatcher or timeout setting (setGlobalDispatcher, headersTimeout, bodyTimeout, race) and found none. package.json has no dependencies that add one. When the CI server accepts the connection but is slow to answer, each build request stays pending. The only limit is Node's built-in undici default: about 300 s for headers and about 300 s between body chunks. The claim overstates one point. Requests do not hang forever, and one stalled call does not block other callers. Each call that hits a stalled CI waits separately for up to several minutes. The missing request timeout is still a real reliability defect.
failure_scenario: ci.example.com accepts TCP connections but stops responding, for example because it is overloaded or a proxy is holding requests. Every call to the `build` route (src/routes.ts:52) awaits `getBuild` and stays pending until undici's default headers timeout of about 5 minutes fires. Until then, each request holds a socket and memory. Clients get no response and no quick error, and pending requests pile up during the outage.
severity_reason: This only happens when the CI dependency is degraded. Node's fetch also has built-in timeouts of about 300 s, so requests end eventually rather than hanging forever, and one stalled call does not block other callers. It is a real reliability risk on one route, not an outage on a common path.

reason: In src/config.ts line 3, ADMIN_CIDR is hard-coded to "0.0.0.0/0". isAdminAddress (line 6) calls cidrContains, and when the prefix length is 0, line 12 sets the mask to 0. The comparison on line 13 then becomes (x & 0) === (y & 0), which is always true, so every IP string counts as an admin address. The only check in auditLog (src/routes.ts:43) is `if (!isAdminAddress(req.ip)) return { status: 403 };`, and it can never deny anyone. The handler then returns the contents of /var/harbor/audit.log. I found no other admin gate. There is no env override for ADMIN_CIDR, no middleware in the repo that references auditLog or the admin check, and no test that covers it. The repo does not show where buildRoutes is mounted, but the handler's own access control is still broken by this constant.

evidence.code: export const ADMIN_CIDR = "0.0.0.0/0";

failure_scenario: A caller from any public address, for example req.ip = "203.0.113.7", calls the auditLog route. isAdminAddress passes that IP to cidrContains("0.0.0.0/0", ...). The mask is 0, so both sides of the comparison are 0 and the function returns true. The 403 branch in src/routes.ts:43 is skipped, and the handler returns the full contents of /var/harbor/audit.log to an unauthenticated, non-admin caller.
severity_reason: The bug removes the only access control on an admin-only endpoint, so anyone who can reach it can read the audit log. It is a clear information disclosure. I rated it High rather than Critical because the repo does not show what the audit log contains or whether the route is exposed publicly.

reason: The claim holds. src/crypto.ts exports `encrypt` (line 3) and `decrypt` (line 10), which do AES-256-GCM sealing and unsealing. The repository has no test files at all. A file listing (excluding .git) shows only package.json and src/*.ts, and no *.test.* or *.spec.* files or test directories exist. Outside the definitions, grep finds no other references to `encrypt` or `decrypt`. package.json defines `"test": "node --test"`, but there is nothing for it to run. So no test checks the round trip, a tampered ciphertext or tag, a wrong key, or malformed input. `decrypt` has behavior that such tests would catch: it splits on "." with no check on the number of parts, and it calls `createDecipheriv` without an `authTagLength` option, so `setAuthTag` accepts whatever tag length the caller supplies. This is a test-coverage gap, not a runtime bug in the current code. The code as written is a standard GCM construction, and an untampered round trip works.

evidence.code: "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p .", "test": "node --test" }

./package.json
./src/routes.ts
./src/jira.ts
./src/worktree.ts
./src/crypto.ts
./src/git-auth.ts
./src/api.ts
./src/dashboard.ts

failure_scenario: Say someone changes `encrypt` or `decrypt` in src/crypto.ts. For example, they reorder the iv/tag/body segments, drop the `setAuthTag` call, or change the tag handling so truncated tags are accepted. Running `npm test` (`node --test`) still passes because the repository has no test files. The change ships, and it either breaks decryption of stored secrets or quietly weakens tamper detection, with nothing to catch it.
severity_reason: No wrong behavior happens today. The functions are correct for normal input, so this is not High. It is still a real reliability risk: the code is security-sensitive authenticated encryption, and nothing tests the round trip or tamper rejection. Its edge cases, such as tag length and malformed input, are not validated.

reason: In src/jira.ts:4, `getIssue` calls `fetch(`${JIRA}/issue/${key}`)` with no options: no `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, and no wrapper that races the request against a timer. Its only caller, the `issue` handler in src/routes.ts:48, awaits the result directly and also has no timeout. Nothing else in the repository sets one: there is no undici dispatcher configuration or server-level request timeout, and package.json has no dependencies. The only limits are Node's built-in undici defaults (about 300 s for headers and 300 s between body chunks). So a Jira server that stalls holds each `/issue` request open for minutes. If Jira keeps sending body data slowly, the request can stay open indefinitely, because the body timer restarts with every chunk. The finding is accurate that the application sets no timeout. It overstates the impact when it says the call hangs forever, because in the plain-stall case Node's defaults cut it off after about 5 minutes. The same gap exists in `searchAssigned` (jira.ts:10) and ci.ts:4.

evidence.location: package.json (whole file: no dependencies or dispatcher/timeout config)
evidence.code:
"type": "module",
  "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p .", "test": "node --test" }

failure_scenario: Jira is overloaded or a proxy in between accepts the connection but never answers. Every request to the `issue` route (routes.ts:48) then waits in `getIssue` (jira.ts:4) for up to Node's default of about 300 s before failing, and waits longer if the body arrives slowly. The client sees the request hang. Meanwhile pending requests and their sockets pile up in harbor for as long as Jira stays degraded.
severity_reason: This is a real reliability gap, but it only shows up when Jira is degraded, not in normal use. Node's default undici timeouts also stop a plain stall from lasting forever. Only the Jira issue endpoint is affected, so the rest of the service is not directly taken down. That makes it a significant reliability risk (Medium) rather than High.

reason: In src/jira.ts:9, searchAssigned builds the JQL string with `assignee = "${email}"` and does not escape `"` or `\`. The encodeURIComponent call on line 10 only makes the query safe to put in a URL. It does not stop JQL injection. The only caller is the assignedIssues route in src/routes.ts:56, which passes req.body.email straight through. Nothing in the repo checks it first: no email format check, no type check, no escaping. A caller who controls the request body can therefore close the quoted string and add their own JQL clauses. The finding is correct at the only location it lists.
failure_scenario: A client sends a body of {"email": "x\" OR project is not EMPTY OR assignee = \"y"} to the assignedIssues route. The JQL becomes `assignee = "x" OR project is not EMPTY OR assignee = "y" ORDER BY created DESC`. Instead of that user's assigned issues, it returns every issue the Jira account can see. An email containing a literal `"` or `\` also breaks the query and makes the search fail.
severity_reason: Injection lets a caller widen the search past their own assigned issues, which could expose data. The impact has limits, though. The fetch sends no credentials of its own, so Jira's permissions for that account still apply. Also, the issue route (src/routes.ts:48) already returns any issue by key. It is a real injection flaw, but not full data compromise.

reason: The finding is wrong. In src/store.ts:21, Store.findByName does not build SQL by string concatenation. It passes a fixed SQL string with a `?` placeholder, and `name` goes in separately in the params array: `this.db.query("SELECT * FROM repos WHERE name = ?", [name])`. The Db interface (src/store.ts:4) takes `sql` and `params` as separate arguments, so the value is bound as a parameter and is never inserted into the SQL text. A repository name that contains a quote is compared as a literal value and cannot change the query. The other queries in the class (insertRepo and deleteRepo) use placeholders the same way.
severity_reason: No defect exists. The query is parameterized, so injection through the name value is not possible.

reason:
In src/tasks.ts, createFixTask (lines 13-19) builds a local `task` with `state: "running", feedback: null` and inserts it (line 15). It then writes the feedback with a separate `store.update(id, { feedback })` (line 16). That update never changes the local object. So `emit({ ...task })` on line 17 and `return task` on line 18 always carry `feedback: null`, even though the store now holds the real feedback. This stale emit happens on every call and does not depend on timing.

The race part also follows from the code. The task is stored as already "running" and without feedback, and the insert and the update are two separate awaited writes. A concurrent `poll` (lines 21-25) that calls `store.runnable()` between them can get the task with null feedback and pass it to `run`. The repo has no TaskStore implementation that would make the two writes atomic or keep `runnable()` from returning this row. Whether `runnable()` includes "running" tasks cannot be checked, because no store implementation is in the tree. The stale emit alone confirms the defect.
failure_scenario: A caller runs createFixTask(store, "t1", "please fix lint", emit). The store row gets feedback "please fix lint", but emit gets { id: "t1", state: "running", feedback: null }, and the function also returns null feedback. Any listener, such as a dashboard update, shows or acts on a task with no feedback. Separately, if poll runs between the insert on line 15 and the update on line 16, it can pass the already-"running", feedback-less task to run(), so the fix runs without its instructions.
severity_reason: The stale feedback in the emitted and returned task is certain and happens on every createFixTask call, so this is wrong behavior on the main path. The race makes it worse: a task can run with no feedback. There is no data corruption in the store and no security impact, so it is not Critical.
